passage:
Fourteen red ticks on the calendar taped inside Hrithik's hostel locker. Fourteen mornings of waking at 5:30, running four rounds of the school ground and doing push-ups while the warden's radio played bhajans.
Today he drew the tick extra thick. "Two weeks, Pankaj," he said, pointing with the marker. "I'm a morning runner now."
Pankaj yawned from the top bunk. "Next week we have the Ooty trip. Three days. What'll you do?"
Hrithik's smile slipped. He hadn't thought about that. "I'll run there."
"In the bus?"
"I'll find a way."
He stared at the neat row of red ticks and felt a small knot in his stomach. The thought of an empty box in the middle of them felt worse than it should.

qa.q: How many red ticks were on Hrithik's calendar?
qa.a: Fourteen red ticks.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik feel a knot in his stomach looking at the calendar?
qa.a: The streak has become part of who he is, a morning runner, so imagining an empty box during the trip felt like it would spoil everything 😰.

qa.q: What could Hrithik plan for the trip so a gap doesn't feel like a disaster?
qa.a: He could decide ahead that trip days are rest days or short walks and mark them differently, so the streak pauses rather than breaks.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Hrithik's new routine?
qa.a: Pankaj seems half impressed and half teasing, and his question about the trip shows he can see the streak will be hard to keep.

grounding: Shows a teenager proud of a two-week running streak that has become part of his identity, and already dreading the first missed day.

passage:
Dear Jagdish Sir,
In the last tuition class you told us to try one fixed hour of maths every day, so I'm writing to report: fifteen days, no gaps! I do 7 to 8 pm at the dining table, with my phone locked in Ammi's cupboard. I've made a chart with gold stars, and I'll admit I love sticking them on more than doing the sums, some days.
My little brother now calls me "Maths Afreen." I pretend to be annoyed, but I'm not.
Only one thing is worrying me. Next week we go to Hyderabad for my cousin's wedding, four days of functions. If I miss even one day, the chart will look ruined, and I think I'll feel like the old me who never stuck to anything.
Is it okay to carry my maths book to a wedding?
Thank you for the idea,
Afreen

qa.q: What time does Afreen do maths each day?
qa.a: From 7 to 8 pm at the dining table.

qa.q: What is Afreen worried about for the wedding trip?
qa.a: Afreen worries that missing even one day will make the chart look ruined and bring back the old self who never stuck to anything.

qa.q: What might Jagdish Sir advise about the four wedding days?
qa.a: He could suggest a short, easy version, like a few minutes of revision, or marking those days as a planned pause, so one gap doesn't undo fifteen days.

qa.q: How does Afreen's little brother seem to see the new routine?
qa.a: He has noticed it enough to give a nickname, 'Maths Afreen', which shows the routine is becoming part of how the family sees Afreen.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager enjoying a fifteen-day study streak that has become part of their identity, and fearing one slip will ruin it.

passage:
In the village near Bathinda, Gurleen had pinned a calendar above her study table. Each evening after two hours of revision for boards, she drew a fat red tick. Fifteen ticks so far.
Her cousin Usha, visiting for the week, noticed. "Fifteen days without a break?"
"Not one," Gurleen said proudly. "I'm the girl who studies every day now."
"What if you go to the wedding on Sunday?"
Gurleen's face fell. "I'll study before. Or after. I can't break it."
"And if you can't?"
Gurleen stared at the calendar. The thought of a blank square made her stomach tighten.

qa.q: How many ticks were on Gurleen's calendar?
qa.a: Fifteen ticks.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she stared at the calendar?
qa.a: She felt anxious, her stomach tightening at the thought of a blank square breaking her streak.

qa.q: What could Gurleen decide now to protect the habit?
qa.a: That a planned break for the wedding is fine, and the habit is about most days, not a perfect streak.

qa.q: How might Usha see Gurleen's pride?
qa.a: Usha seems impressed but gently concerned that the streak has become too rigid.

grounding: Shows a teen proud of a fifteen-day study streak that has become her identity, and anxious that one break would ruin it.

passage:
In Kraków, Olga had done forty push-ups every morning for sixteen days. She marked each day on the calendar by the door with a gold star.
"You're obsessed," said her sister Ada, eating cereal.
"I'm disciplined," Olga said, on push-up thirty-eight. "I'm a fitness person now."
"We're going to Babcia's for the weekend. There's no space there."
Olga stopped at thirty-nine. "I'll do them in the hallway."
"And if you can't?"
"Then the streak's gone." She said it like the end of the world.
Ada shrugged. "It's push-ups, Olga. Not a religion."

qa.q: How many days had Olga done push-ups?
qa.a: Sixteen days.

qa.q: What was Olga feeling when she said the streak would be gone?
qa.a: She felt anxious and alarmed, as if one missed day would be a disaster for the fitness person she now saw herself as.

qa.q: What could help Olga keep the habit through the weekend away?
qa.a: A smaller version, like a few push-ups in the hallway, and accepting that one missed day doesn't undo the habit.

qa.q: How does Ada see Olga's streak?
qa.a: Ada finds it a bit much and teases her, seeing the streak as more important to Olga than it needs to be.

grounding: Shows a teen proud of a sixteen-day push-up streak that has become her identity, and fearing one missed day as a disaster.

passage: In Room 14 of the boys' hostel, a calendar hung beside Wasim's bunk with fourteen fat green ticks. Every morning since the first of the month he had been up at 5:45 for revision before the bell, and every night he ticked the day with a satisfied click of the pen. "Streak king," Hemant called him, and Wasim liked the name more than he admitted. He had started telling juniors, "I'm a morning person now." On day fifteen the warden announced a late-night inter-house quiz, and afterwards Wasim lay awake staring at the calendar. If he slept through the alarm, the fifteenth box would stay empty. The thought made his stomach turn, as if one blank square would cancel all fourteen ticks and prove he had never really changed.

qa.q: How many ticks were on Wasim's calendar?
qa.a: Fourteen fat green ticks.

qa.q: Why did the thought of an empty box make Wasim's stomach turn?
qa.a: He feels anxious because the streak has become who he is, so one miss feels like proof he never changed.

qa.q: What could Wasim tell himself about a possible missed morning?
qa.a: That one blank square after a late quiz is a normal slip, and restarting the next morning keeps the habit alive.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Wasim's streak?
qa.a: Hemant seems to admire it, teasing him fondly as the streak king, perhaps without seeing the pressure it adds.

grounding: Shows a teen proud of a two-week routine that has become part of who he is, so a single possible slip feels like a disaster.
